Expected Goals Model Evaluation

Calibration








Figure 9: Calibration plot for the MoneyPuck xG model. Points close to the diagonal indicate well-calibrated predictions.







Brier Score
The overall Brier score for the xG model is 0.0538, indicating moderate predictive accuracy. For reference, a perfect model scores 0 and a model predicting the overall goal rate for every shot scores approximately 0.0629.


Team-Level Residuals








Figure 10: Team-level actual goals vs. expected goals (xG). Teams above the line scored more than expected; teams below scored fewer.







Top Shooters: Actual vs. Expected








Figure 11: Top 20 shooters by shot volume, comparing actual goals to expected goals (xG). Red bars exceed expectations; blue bars fall short.

title: Analysis
text:
Simple Logistic Regression Model








Figure 12: Coefficient plot from logistic regression model predicting goal probability.





The logistic regression achieves a deviance of 9.17487^{5} on 2,074,837 residual degrees of freedom. Key findings:

Shot distance has a strong negative coefficient: each additional foot from the net reduces the log-odds of a goal.
Shot angle has a moderate negative effect: wider angles (shots from the periphery) are less dangerous.
Rush shots and rebounds substantially increase goal probability.
Snap shots and tips/deflections outperform wrist shots, while slap shots perform similarly.

title: Analysis
text:
Conclusion
This analysis reveals several key findings about NHL shot quality:

Scoring rates have been relatively stable over 19 seasons, hovering around 9–10% per shot, with no dramatic league-wide trend despite the analytics revolution narrative.
Shot location dominates scoring probability. The slot (close range, centered angle) remains by far the most dangerous area. Shots from inside 20 feet convert at nearly three times the rate of shots from 30+ feet.
Rush and rebound situations are high-value. Rush shots and rebounds produce meaningfully higher goal rates than standard shots, suggesting that transition play and second-chance opportunities are critical to scoring.
The xG model is reasonably well-calibrated, though it tends to slightly underpredict goals at the highest probability levels.
Individual shooter deviations from xG reveal potential over- and under-performers, though isolating this from contextual factors (quality of chances, team system) would require additional analysis.


Limitations

The 2012 lockout and 2020 COVID seasons had fewer games; per-shot rates are used to mitigate this, but per-game comparisons should be made cautiously.
The xG model is a black box from MoneyPuck. We evaluate its output but cannot inspect its internals.
No game-state context (score differential, time remaining) is incorporated into our simple model.
The data includes regular season and playoff games without distinction in most analyses (though isPlayoffGame is available).

title: Where Do Goals Come From?
text:
How have NHL shot profiles and scoring rates changed across 19 seasons (2007–2025), and what shot characteristics best predict goals? This analysis uses shot-level play-by-play data from MoneyPuck spanning 2,079,377 shot events to examine the evolution of shot selection in the modern NHL, evaluate an expected goals (xG) model, and identify which shot characteristics most strongly predict scoring.
The so-called “analytics revolution” in hockey has emphasized shot quality over shot quantity. We investigate whether the data supports this narrative by tracking how shot distances, angles, types, and rush/rebound rates have shifted over time.

title: About
text: This analysis uses shot-level play-by-play data from MoneyPuck, covering 2,079,377 shot events across 19 NHL seasons (2007–2025). The dataset includes precomputed expected goals (xG) values from MoneyPuck’s proprietary model.

title: About
text: This analysis uses shot-level play-by-play data from MoneyPuck, covering 2,079,377 shot events across 19 NHL seasons (2007–2025). The dataset includes precomputed expected goals (xG) values from MoneyPuck’s proprietary model.

title: About
text:
Methodology

Shot data was loaded from individual season CSV files (2007–2025) and combined into a single analysis dataset.
Scoring rates are calculated as goals per shot (not per game) to normalize across shortened seasons (2012 lockout, 2020 COVID).
Shot quality is assessed using distance, angle, shot type, rush/rebound status, and empty net indicators.
The xG model is evaluated using calibration plots, Brier scores, and team/shooter-level residual analysis.
A simple logistic regression (goal ~ distance + angle + shotType + rebound + rush + emptyNet) is fitted to identify which characteristics most strongly predict scoring.
